items.title: My AI agents found an unmapped Maya site
items.content:
Update (11 November): it turns out the site had already been mapped in Estrada-Belli et al. 2025 . The agents missed it while going through the literature, so they rediscovered it rather than discovered it (it just wasn't in the register of Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History, INAH, yet). Still work to do then! The rest of the story still holds.

By analyzing NASA lidar data, my AI agents found a Maya site in Mexico that wasn't in the official register. (It turned out archaeologists had mapped it already, more on that at the end.) It took less than 72 hours to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive.

I'm going to tell this story as a diary, because the timeline is probably the best part.

I was traveling in Peru, Gemini-ing about the history of the place, when I learned about Hiram Bingham , the American explorer who "discovered" Machu Picchu in 1911. "What luck!" I thought. He was actually looking for a different city, Vilcabamba , the last refuge of the Incas, when a local farmer in the valley below guided him to the ruins. "Imagine if Bingham had our tools," I thought. "What would he do?"

I brainstormed a bit with a few agents (Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok), and they all said lidar . From above, a ruin in the jungle is just a bunch of trees (like Machu Picchu before it was cleared), so satellite photos don't help much. Lidar, instead, fires laser pulses through the gaps in the canopy and maps the ground underneath. [1]

So the agents went looking for lidar data. Peru isn't well covered, and hiring a company to do a survey meant permits, costs and bureaucracy, so I gave up on that. Then I thought: why not the Maya ? Their region is much better covered by public lidar.

That night, I asked the agents to analyze it and went to bed.

I woke up and checked the agents' reports. 'DAMN!' They had found lots of villages and other regular shapes that looked like structures or houses.

So how did they do it? They turned the lidar strips (about 1,200 km² of jungle) into images, and 48 agents went through them one by one like very patient archaeologists, looking for pyramids, platforms, and plazas while filtering out natural hills, sinkholes, and roads. There was no special model or classifier involved: the agents literally looked at the pictures, following a precise guide.

Me: That's awesome! Please check which of these villages haven't been discovered yet. Search both the literature and the archives.

Agent: One major village doesn't seem to have been registered.

This is the hilltop from the top of this post. It sits on the edge of a cliff, under the jungle, and it has straight edges and sharp corners. Nature doesn't really do straight lines.

Zooming in, there's a levelled plaza, an oval pyramid at least 8–12 m tall, a raised courtyard attached to it and a flat-bottomed hollow that might have been a water reservoir.

Agent: You should contact INAH (Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History), write a report on your discovery, and check whether the site is in their register. Sometimes they have unpublished results.

Me: OK, how do I contact INAH? How does the reporting process work?

Agent: …instructions for the report… + email addresses

I iterated on the report a bit, since a few things were off, and translated it into Spanish to improve the chances of getting a reply (at least, that's what Claude suggested). I don't speak Spanish, so I had to trust the agents on that one.

The agents also checked the raw point cloud, to make sure the shapes were really on the ground and not created by the trees. Green dots are leaves, brown dots are the ground.

INAH replied: they checked their records and found no registered archaeological site at that location .

At that point I thought nobody had put it on a map before. I was wrong (see below).

items.content_ko:
정정 글: 해당 유적은 Estrada-Belli et al. 2025에 이미 지도화되어 있었다. 에이전트가 문헌을 검토하며 이를 놓쳤기에 새로 발견한 것이 아니라 다시 찾아낸 셈이며, 멕시코 국립인류학역사연구소(INAH) 등록부에는 아직 없었다. 필자는 그래도 할 일이 남아 있고 나머지 내용은 유효하다고 덧붙였다.

본문: 필자는 여행 중 Gemini와 페루의 역사를 이야기하다가, 1911년 마추픽추를 '발견'한 미국인 탐험가 Hiram Bingham을 알게 됐다. Bingham은 사실 잉카의 마지막 피난처인 빌카밤바를 찾고 있었는데, 계곡 아래 사는 한 농부의 안내로 유적을 보게 됐다고 한다. 필자는 Bingham이 지금의 도구를 가졌다면 어땠을지 떠올렸다. 이후 AI 에이전트 작업으로 유적을 찾아내 멕시코 정부의 공식 답변까지 받기까지 72시간이 채 걸리지 않았다고 주장한다. 글은 일기 형식으로 전개된다.

items.title: How do you actually self-host securely?
items.content:
I recognize that the title is rather vague, but I'm completely green when it comes to self-hosting, so I figured here would be a good place to ask for some pointers given the discussions I sometimes see happening in the comments. I tried researching first through DDG and Google, but (and I recognize this might be a skill issue) most things I found are either SEO slop or trying to sell/market some service.

For some more context and to give a concrete example as to what I'm interested in, I got my hands on a Raspberry Pi which I'd like to use to start tinkering with self-hosting. My main goal would be to host my (static) website on it, potentially adding more things in the future.

Some people I asked this question recommended solutions like Cloudflare Tunnels to make it secure, but using such a provider almost feels like it defeats the point of self-hosting, so I'm curious whether it's viable to do it using open source tooling, any gotchas one might encounter, and generally any thoughts you might have on the topic.

(Also, feel free to suggest a tag other than devops , I figured security doesn't quite apply since it's a question and not a write-up/resource regarding security.)

It sounds like what you may want is "nobody can read my packets but me!" If that's the case I would look at the chain of things.

These three are super intertwined, "self hosting" is choosing which of these you want to own.

You may end up using nginx or haproxy somewhere to get ports to line up. But you can also use iptables. Dealer's choice.

Tailscale and Cloudflare tunnels are really cool. They take a bit of the headache away, but you're right that they give up that bit of security (and the learning!).

I'm so psyched for you :) let me know how it goes!

I always picture it baking in the sun on the cracked back dash of a 1996 Toyota Camry flying down the highway.

I have to admit that I smiled at this too.

I just drove across the Untied States with my backup MX. My phone provided a hotspot, a GL.inet did tethering and provided Internet, and my backup MX ran a tinc tunnel to give itself a public IP.

Since my backup MX runs off of 5 volts (USB powered) and has a battery backup, I ran it off of the cigarette lighter USB power adapter, but it could've just as easily been off my solar panel (which I run through the hatchback window :)

I'm not sure if acme.sh is the best choice .

Also, for a lot of self-hosting setups (where you've got a server at home with services that you want to reach from other devices), I'd argue that Tailscale is overkill. Plain Wireguard is pleasantly simple to configure.

Sure, it has some niceties - it has NAT traversal, it's smart enough to figure out more efficient routing than the star topology you'd probably end up with in the simplest plain wg setup, it has fancy multiple user support - but do you actually need any of that?

The reason (the only reason!) I'm using Tailscale instead of WireGuard is that Tailscale has native apps all over the place (including critically for Apple TV and Google's streamer-du-jour), whereas WireGuard doesn't.[1]. Given I don't have to pay anything to use Tailscale, that makes it worth it for me for at least that specific use-case.

[1]: Well, there's a paid subscription app for the Apple TV, and I could jailbreak the Google thing, but there's a limit to how much effort I wanna put into just getting my Jellyfin files available.

WireGuard is available on tvOS. Plain, free, open source WireGuard.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

items.title: What are some "No AI" apps/companies/resources you know of?
items.content:
Hey everyone I'm wondering if there's any useful/helpful list of apps, companies, or resources in general that avoid AI (they don't have to be vocally or openly "anti", but at least explicitly avoid it) that you know of?

I'm not looking to start a discussion on what's good/bad or (un)worthy about AI, or who's for/against, just links and/or communities promoting this sentiment/position.

For example, https://www.rebeltechalliance.org would be one of those resources.

https://codeberg.org/ethical-foss/ai-free-foss-alternatives

It's such a shame that a list titled "AI-free FOSS Alternatives" ends up becoming the opposite of its stated goal, with the top level section being "Tainted Software" and occasional sporadic little notes listing alternatives.

I like the steadfast anti-AI people even though I'm not really one of them, and I want them to thrive and carve out a lasting space online. Putting more focus on the positives of the anti-AI vision and way less on the rejection and refusal stuff would probably help with that, and I think this is a really clear example where the negative side of the message has stolen the show unnecessarily. The "tainted" list is inside baseball stuff and belongs in the equivalent of a Wikipedia talk page on there.

I strongly agree that it is better to fight for something good rather than against something bad. However, I find the list a very useful starting point. Studying it led me to the (startling to me) conclusion that the GNU/FSF vision is a positive one that encompasses the rejection of AI. There are probably others as well, but starting with GNU is not starting from scratch at least. Flipping positions on GNU was not on my personal philosophy bingo card for this year.

Putting more focus on the positives of the anti-AI vision and way less on the rejection and refusal stuff would probably help with that,

As a general rule, I think that "focus on the positives" is a good rule of thumb.

As a blanket rule, it doesn't work. Sometimes it's really about the negatives. If you're trying to convince people, say, not to smoke or do heroin... really, "it's great not being addicted to things" is not as strong a message as "you'll get lung cancer if you smoke" or "this is what heroin addiction does to people". (Granted "just say no" was also terrible as a campaign, but for different reasons.)

I'm not saying that AI usage is equivalent to heroin usage, exactly, but I'm not sure that "the positives of the anti-AI vision" is as persuasive as the arguments against generative AI.

where the negative side of the message has stolen the show unnecessarily

Again, I don't really agree with this. There are some things that it makes sense to be against . This is especially true in the case of generative AI in my opinion because of the way it spreads and has basically overrun the industry in a couple of years. For some of us, it's the black mold or asbestos of software. "Gee, having a house without black mold is so awesome" isn't really quite the same as "here's what black mold is going to do to you if it infests your house".

This list used to be called Open Slopware. I wrote about my personal relationship to it here: https://lobste.rs/s/unpaan/arborium_is_ai_slopware_should_not_be#c_twqzh3 .

Mmmm not terribly surprising unfortunately.

I think this is a common kind of unspoken ethical framework where if you're decently progressive and/or in any way marginalised then you're ontologically incapable of being abusive because your shitty behaviour is actually all just righteous anger and moral courage and any critique you receive is actually just so much privileged tone policing. I used to subscribe to this way of thinking too and have moved on from it but it's especially popular in the anti-AI activism sphere at the moment.

Wrote down a few of my thoughts about it the other day actually.

Being overtly nasty might make you feel alive for a moment but it’s in conflict with any meaningful real-world goals, and…

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: 대기업 총수, 의장 경제문제 때문에 못조져 놓는다는 건
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

마치 테러리스트가 인질극 벌이는데 인질 죽는다고 테러리스트 진압 안하겠다는 것과 같은 말이다.

총수, 의장 검찰 총원해서 조져 놓다가 사면을 해놓으니까 버릇이 안좋아 진건지 아니면 반도체좀 했다고 뭐가 된양인지 모르겠다만

앞으로 대한민국에서도 여당과 야당 합작으로 대기업 총수, 의장 사법처리하고 사면하지않고 만기 출소하는 케이스가 단 한 번이라도 나와서 명확하게 그 선례를 남겨놔야한다는게 내 생

items.title: AWS emulator
items.content:
AWS Emulator is a local emulator of the AWS APIs. You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI). You don’t need an AWS account. Your requests go to the emulator, not to AWS. So you work with emulated resources instead of AWS resources. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS.

The emulator is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint. It has no graphical interface. After you start the emulator, you set environment variables to point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at its endpoint. Then you run your code as usual. In embedded mode, you pass the emulator’s HTTP client to your SDK instead.

AWS Emulator is for building and testing. Don’t use it for production workloads or to test security. See Security in AWS Emulator .

Install the aws-emulator skill, then ask your agent to set up the emulator. This needs the AWS CLI version 2.35.0 or later. See Getting started with an AI coding agent .

aws agent-toolkit add-skill --skill-name aws-emulator --region us-east-1

Linux: install the RPM or Debian package and run aws-emulator . See Getting started on Linux .

Windows / macOS: run the emulator in a container built from a short Dockerfile. See Getting started with Docker .

Point your SDK at a running emulator by setting environment variables. See Pointing your AWS SDK at AWS Emulator .

Add the emulator as a dev-dependency and run it in-process, one isolated instance per test. There is no endpoint URL, certificate, or environment variable to set. Your test wires the emulator's HTTP client straight into the SDK client. See Getting started with embedded mode , and Building from source below for its build cost.

To see how closely each service matches AWS, check the fidelity scores published with each release on the releases page . To check whether your own project is expected to work, see Checking whether your project works with AWS Emulator .

Individual gaps are tracked in the repository's issues/ directory. APIs and behaviors that don't work yet are under issues/things-that-do-not-work/ , and ones that have since been fixed move to issues/things-that-now-work/ .

You need this if you are modifying the emulator, running it from a checkout, or using embedded mode. Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so the prerequisites and build-cost guidance below apply to it too. Most other users install a prebuilt package instead (see Quick start ). Building from source is supported on Linux (x86_64 and aarch64) ; on Windows and macOS, use the Docker path above.

A Rust toolchain with Cargo (install via rustup ).

A C compiler, such as GCC or clang. Some dependencies build C code.

At least 100 GB of free disk for target/ . The workspace has one crate per AWS service, so a debug build of everything is large, and it grows as services are added.

A multi-core machine. A cold full build compiles every service crate, so the first build takes a while; fewer cores take proportionally longer. After that, rebuilding after a change to one service is much faster.

The emulator serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 (self-signed certificate).

Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so your project's first cargo test builds the emulator's service crates alongside your own code. Budget a first build and target/ on the same order as building from source above, then fast incremental builds. Recommendation: reuse one CARGO_TARGET_DIR across projects, cache target/ (or use sccache) in CI, and pin the emulator to a release commit so it isn't rebuilt on every change.

├── Cargo.toml # workspace: one member per service, plus the core crates

│ └── service-<name>/ # ONE CRATE PER SERVICE

│ ├── smithy-model/ # <name>.json — the Smithy model that drives the wire protocol

│ ├── build.rs # generates the service declaration from the model

│ │ ├── service.rs # request routing and refusal…

items.title: How a false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Street's only NYC datacenter
items.content:
AI disclosure: this story was written entirely by human hands, with AI doing proof-reading and light edits. Some tasteful imperfections kept to heighten Wabi-Sabi effect.

Everyone’s heard of how awesome Jane Street is. Fewer people have heard about the times something stupid nearly put it out of business and it was saved by grit and dumb luck. I was on the systems team for some of those. Jane Street didn’t do titles, and we on the systems team weren’t above getting our hands dirty. You could think of us as the firm’s blue-collar OCaml programmers: when something broke, we were the ones running through the corridors to fix it. Call this story a Star Trek: Lower Decks view of Jane Street.

For the longest time Jane Street insisted on having its machine room close to its trading floor. When it was 10 people it was cute. When it was 150 people it was starting to feel… odd. Part of the reason for this was intellectual property concern: they didn’t want to risk having their servers stolen by spies who would learn their precious trading strategies. Another reason was technology risk: they wanted to make sure out-of-control automated trading systems could always be shut down by running across the hall and pulling power cables.

Yes, tools existed to mitigate both of these fears. But Jane Street moved irritatingly slowly on this stuff, and they still wanted the last-resort option of yanking power cords. Their risk culture didn’t exclusively come from reading heady thinkpieces. A lot of it was instilled by a partner who’d served on a nuclear submarine, and it showed, mostly in a good way! On a sub, you don’t trust the automation unless there’s a big red-painted, mechanically connected lever you can pull to turn it off.

As the company grew this humble machine room was built out into a respectably sizable datacenter, complete with an online UPS, Computer Room Air Conditioner (CRAC) units, refrigerator-sized network switches, a subterranean diesel backup generator and about 10 rows of server cabinets, 10 cabinets deep. Oh, and it was all crammed into the middle of a skyscraper called 1 New York Plaza , which was otherwise just a normal office building.

When I first landed my job at Jane Street I was commuting to the southern tip of Manhattan all of the way from Queens, an hour or more each way. I’d gone to a magnet high school in the city, so I’d been doing commutes like that since I was a teenager, and I was tired of it.

Now that I was making big Wall Street money I decided I’d get an apartment. A real estate agent kept trying to show me what they called “panty droppers”, but I was only interested in one thing: proximity to the office. I ended up in a 200 square foot studio that was a 9 minute commute on foot from my apartment door to my desk on the trading floor. I would weirdly boast about it to the rest of the systems team, but it also meant everyone at the office knew I was a stone’s throw away in case there was an emergency.

And that day came soon enough. One evening after work, just as I was about to climb into the elevator at my apartment building, my phone rang. It was our Hong Kong office, and when Hong Kong had a New York problem, mine was (now) the number they called. The smoke alarm in our NYC datacenter had gone off.

We had contractors working on a prep room next to the datacenter. While cutting into stuff, some dust was kicked up and it set off the smoke alarm. This is bad, but not for the reason you might think. Office buildings have sprinklers in them for fire suppression. You may have seen it go off in movies where someone just holds a lit cigarette up to the sprinkler on the ceiling and it floods the entire room. In reality they’re not quite that dumb, but it’s close.

Firstly, the sprinklers over a machine room like ours usually aren’t kept full of water all of the time. This saves you from having to deal with any leaks that might develop overhead over the years. Secondly, the sprinkler heads don’t have smoke…

items.title: Nvidia CEO Huang allegedly involved in a second affair with an Nvidia exec
items.content:
Nvidia CEO Huang allegedly involved in a second affair with an Nvidia exec

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks to the media and attendees after a reception celebrating the UK's technology ecosystem and AI advances in London, Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. (AP Photo/Kwiyeon Ha) · Yahoo Finance · AP Photo/Kwiyeon Ha

Thu, November 12, 2026 at 7:43 AM GMT+9 1 min read

Embattled Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang was allegedly involved in a second extramarital affair.

The company's board is reportedly meeting to determine if it will oust Huang as chief executive, the Wall Street Journal reports .

Nvidia stock fell in after-hours trading following the report.

According to The New York Times , Huang, whose relationship with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy has embroiled the company in scandal this week, also had a relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell.

She joined Nvidia in 2008 and heads up the company's healthcare business.

The Times report says that Huang and Powell were seen being affectionate at a hotel during a company conference in March, and that when a bystander took a photo of the interaction, a security guard "sequestered them" and made them an offer to sign a nondisclosure agreement.

Last month, The Times reported that US intelligence services believed a woman, Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, may have acted as an intelligence asset , sharing information with the ruling party in Beijing.

On Sunday, Huang issued a statement apologizing to his family and Nvidia employees for having an affair, though he didn't name with whom.

In response, Nvidia's board said it is launching an independent investigation into the matter.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the board said in a statement Sunday.

items.title: Band-aid accessibility
items.content:
More and more disabled people take matters into their own hand and use LLM 1

coding tools to generate accessible features or wholly accessible app for their use cases. While it seems easy to celebrate this as an act of liberation for these users, reality is more complicated.

I'm a web accessibility professional who cares deeply about inclusion and an open web for everyone. I work with Axess Lab as an accessibility specialist. Previously, I worked with Knowbility , the World Wide Web Consortium , and Aktion Mensch . In this blog I publish my own thoughts and research about the web industry.

Sign up for a €5/Month Membership Subscribe to the Infrequent Newsletter Follow me on Mastodon

I support everyone to get the access needed, even if this is via dubious, unethical, or illegal ways. I can't fault someone with chronic pain who finds relief in cannabis. I won't judge anyone who needs to find "alternative ways" to get books that work for them and their disabilities, and who cannot read DRM 2

-laden books. And I don't find fault with anyone who removes barriers using LLM coding tools.

There is a lot of debate, mainly on Mastodon 3

, about the ethics of creating(?) accessible apps this way. And a lot of these arguments, I can relate to:

Disabled people have always been ignored by most mainstream software developers and companies.

Years of begging to make interfaces accessible, particularly to screen readers and for their users, lead to nothing.

This is a way users can ensure access in a timely way.

Screen reader users know better how interfaces work for them and can "prompt" to meet these requirements.

The projects might not be sustainable in the long run.

Not using mainstream software creates parallel spaces for disabled people.

Software developers might do less accessibility, because disabled people can just patch it after the fact.

Commercial LLM vendors use these projects to accessibility-wash their ethical problems.

The state of accessibility is dire. I review dozens of projects every year, and the quality has rarely been as low – with notable exceptions! – than in 2026. And this doesn't even cover only accessibility issues: It looks like most software is not tested at all, be it for functionality or error handling, or just stability. Everything breaks all the time.

And what is an inconvenience to some users is a barrier to others. 4

As a LLM skeptic, I see a lot of the risks outlined above myself. It would never be for me to use an LLM to create something. I enjoy the creating and the problem solving too much, and honestly as an accessibility reviewer, you often get the "identifying problems" but hardly ever the "problem solving" side of the coin. It can be very frustrating.

But this is for many screen reader users the first time they feel that they have tools they can use to solve accessibility problems by themselves for themselves. I always wondered why there are not more disabled, and especially blind, programmers around, and I assume the reasons are ableist structures around computer education.

But even then, letting a blind developer lead your website or app UI development? Probably unimaginable in most companies. UI means painting it nicely, right?

My real worry is about the long-term sustainability of this approach. Creating separate paths often means features get out of sync. Rising cost of LLM code generators will also limit what can be done on a budget. Which also makes these kinds of developments, as accessible as the result may be, burden with a disability tax. And that might even increase once companies de-prioritize accessibility work because supposedly the community will take care of it.

What I hope this does is for disabled people to be interested in coding more, but we also need the other side to go and do the work: It can't be that accessibility issues are pushed later for years and years and years.

No doubt, the community is creating some extremely good band-aids, but it is…

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

제가 집에서 한 말이나 제 언니랑 한 말들을 학교 가면 다 알고있어요 그래서 제가 말한 내용이랑 똑같은 내용을 꼭 제가 들을 수 있을때 언급하고 남자애들 여자애들 할것없이 제가 안보이는 데에서 조금만 이상한 말 하면 비웃으면서 지나가요 ㅠ 제가 진짜 친구가 없어서 학교에서 한마디도 안하는 날들이 대부분인데 제가 언니랑 학교 구석에서 말한 내용이랑 집에서 혼잣말 한 내용들을 똑같이 언급한게 한두번이 아니에요 ㅠ 제가 그냥 내용만 겹치면 말을 않겠는데 제가 말했던 내용 언급하면서 꼭 제 이름도 한번씩 부르고 그래요 보통 사람들은 자기이름을 그렇게 말하면 기분나빠서 한번 돌아보기라도 하겠지만 저는 성격이 워낙 내성적이라 누가 비웃고 지나가거나 째려보거나 저 보면서 한숨쉬어도 아무말도 못하거든요 ㅠ 그래서 그냥 기분만 나쁜건데 이게 하루이틀 쌓이니까 너무 힘들더라고요 ㅠ 처음엔 저도 이게 정신이 약간 아픈건가 했는데 정신병 관련 영상도 다 보고 그랬는데 환청은 이런식으로 들리는게 아니라고 하더라고요 계속 날 비난하고 그런식으로 들리는건데 저는 그런게 전혀 아니라 제가 전날 했던 얘기들, 방금 쉬는시간에 학교 구석에서 나눈 얘기들을 자꾸 똑같이 언급하니까 미치겠어요 ㅠ 한두번 우연으로 겹치는게 아니라 계속 겹쳐요 진짜.. 그리고 애초에 제가 학교에서 말을 한마디도 안하는데 자꾸 저한테 그런 반응을 보인다는게 애초에 저한테 이상한 일이 일어난다는 반증 아닌가요? 그리고 걔네가 말했던걸 몇개를 말씀드려보면 제가 도청을 의심한 초기에 급식실에서 밥먹고있었는데 어떤 남자애가 “도청” 이러고 지나가는거에요 그리고 저희반 남자애가 제 언니 이동수업반이랑 같은 반인데 거기서 쉬는시간에 “도청기를 달고다녀 ㅋㅋㅋㅋ” 이랬다는거에요 진짜 이상하죠 저는 예전에 우울증 약을 먹은적이 있어서 정신이 막 무결점으로 건강한 편은 아니에요 근데 저희 언니는 그런적도 없고 교우관계도 좋고 진짜 정신이 건강하거든요 ㅠ 근데 저희 언니가 그런말을 들었다니깐 진짜 도청이 일어나는게 맞는거구나 생각했어요.. 그리고 또 있었던 일을 말씀드리면 이동수업 때 제 뒷쪽에서 남자애가 제 아버지 직업을 언급하면서 제 이름을 말하는거에요 이게 도청을 하지 않고서는 절대 알수가 없는 사실이거든요 ㅠ 또 “정신병ㅋㅋㅋ” 하면서 제 이름을 언급하는거에요 이것도 도청을 하지 않았다면 알수 없는거고요 더 말씀드릴 사례가 많은데 그러면 너무 길어져서 이정도만 말씀드릴게요 그래서 찾아보니까 머리에 붙일수 있는 초소형 도청기가 있다길래  제 언니가 제 머리를 샅샅이 뒤져줬거든요? 근데 그래도 아무것도 안나오더라고요 ㅠ 그리고 또 도청 탐지 업체를 알아보니까 금액이 너무 비싸서요 ㅠ 제가 고3인데 이런일을 당해서 너무 스트레스 받는데 방법이 없어서 정말 어떻게 해야될지 모르겠어요 안그래도 제가 여자애들이나 남자애들이 괴롭힐 소재가 많은 조용한 애거든요 ㅠ그래서 저를 지나칠때 꼭 한마디 끼얹고 지나가고 그래서 학교생활이 막 편한 그런애는 아닌데 학교에서 유일하게 맘놓고 말할 수 있는 언니랑 말하는 얘기를 다 알고있으니까 스트레스 받아서 공부 능력도 점점 떨어지는것같고 쨋든 걱정이 이만저만이 아니에요 어떡해야되죠 ㅠㅠ 제가 성격이 활발한 편도 아니고 집에 돈이 많지도 않아서 진짜 대학 잘가야되는데 걱정이에요ㅠㅠ 긴글 읽어주셔서 감사하고요 여기가 사생활 침해 관련한 갤러리니까 혹여나 저랑 비슷한 경험이 있으시거나 관련 지식이 있는 분은 제가 어떻게 해야하는건지 알려주시면 진짜진짜 감사드릴것같아요 많은 도움 부탁드려요 정말 방법 여러가지 찾아봐도 안되겠어서 여기다 글 남겨요

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Day 9 - Diving into networking
items.content:
The two services your server is now running are sshd for remote login, and apache2 for web access. These are both “open to the world” via the TCP/IP “ports” - 22 and 80.

As a sysadmin, you need to understand what ports you have open on your servers because each open port is also a potential focus of attacks. You need to be be able to put in place appropriate monitoring and controls.

Secure your web server by using a firewall

First we’ll look at a couple of ways of determining what ports are open on your server:

ss - this, “socket status”, is a standard utility - replacing the older netstat

nmap - this “port scanner” won’t normally be installed by default

There are a wide range of options that can be used with ss , but first try: ss -ltpn

The output lines show which ports are open on which interfaces:

State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:Port Process

LISTEN 0 4096 127.0.0.53%lo:53 0.0.0.0:* users:(("systemd-resolve",pid=364,fd=13))

LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:22 0.0.0.0:* users:(("sshd",pid=625,fd=3))

LISTEN 0 128 [::]:22 [::]:* users:(("sshd",pid=625,fd=4))

LISTEN 0 511 *:80 * :* users:(("apache2",pid=106630,fd=4),("apache2",pid=106629,fd=4),("apache2",pid=106627,fd=4))

The network notation can be a little confusing, but the lines above show ports 80 and 22 open “to the world” on all local IP addresses - and port 53 (DNS) open only on a special local address.

Now install nmap with apt install . This works rather differently, actively probing 1,000 or more ports to check whether they’re open. It’s most famously used to scan remote machines - please don’t - but it’s also very handy to check your own configuration, by scanning your server:

Starting Nmap 5 .21 ( http://nmap.org ) at 2013 -03-17 02 :18 UTC

Nmap scan report for localhost ( 127 .0.0.1 )

Nmap done : 1 IP address ( 1 host up ) scanned in 0 .08 seconds

Port 22 is providing the ssh service, which is how you’re connected, so that will be open. If you have Apache running then port 80/http will also be open. Every open port is an increase in the “attack surface”, so it’s Best Practice to shut down services that you don’t need.

Note that however that “localhost” (127.0.0.1), is the loopback network device. Services “bound” only to this will only be available on this local machine. To see what’s actually exposed to others, first use the ip a command to find the IP address of your actual network card, and then nmap that.

The Linux kernel has built-in firewall functionality called “netfilter”. We configure and query this via various utilities, the most low-level of which are the iptables command, and the newer nftables . These are powerful, but also complex - so we’ll use a more friendly alternative - ufw - the “uncomplicated firewall”.

First let’s list what rules are in place by typing sudo iptables -L

So, essentially no firewalling - any traffic is accepted to anywhere.

Using ufw is very simple. It is available by default in all Ubuntu installations after 8.04 LTS, but if you need to install it:

Then, to allow SSH, but disallow HTTP we would type:

BEWARE! Don’t forget to explicitly ALLOW ssh , or you’ll lose all contact with your server! If not allowed, the firewall assumes the port is DENIED by default.

Typing sudo iptables -L now will list the detailed rules generated by this - one of these should now be:

“DROP tcp -- anywhere anywhere tcp dpt:http”

The effect of this is that although your server is still running Apache, it’s no longer accessible from the “outside” - all incoming traffic to the destination port of http/80 being DROPed. Test for yourself! You will probably want to reverse this with:

In practice, ensuring that you’re not running unnecessary services is often enough protection, and a host-based firewall is unnecessary, but this very much depends on the type of server you are configuring. Regardless, hopefully this session has given you some insight into the concepts.

items.title: Using voltage glitching to unleash the A100 in my mining card
items.content:
Using voltage glitching to unleash the A100 in my mining card

View more blogs with the tag  hardware , View more blogs with the tag  security

I’ve discovered a voltage fault injection vulnerability on the GA100 die, allowing an operator to blow arbitrary fuses. Utilizing this vulnerability, I’ve converted my CMP 170HX 8GB card into what is effectively an A100-80G! Further, my unlocked cards actually perform ~1.2x faster than a retail A100 by having all functional SMs enabled (~120-126, die-lottery dependent), rather than the yield-safe 108 SMs NVIDIA chose for all production A100 cards. Finally, CMP-disabled features like NVLink, PCIe Gen4, NVJPG, NVDEC, MIG are all unlockable with this approach, though I haven’t specifically tested NVJPG/NVDEC/MIG.

Here’s how my “A100-80G” appears and functions.

NVIDIA uses fuses for product segmentation, security features, and other fun access control features - and crucially, there are several functions where blowing a fuse on an NVIDIA die can grant you more access, not less. In a properly secured design, a blown fuse should always induce a more restrictive state, because a blown fuse cannot be unblown in an economically feasible way. NVIDIA’s design allows one to relax restrictions by blowing more fuses!

In this post, I will go over the GA100 die, its fuse controller, the use of VFI, and future research directions. I’ve decided to publish some of the work that enabled my research here .

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: AI has made developers more powerful than ever. Why aren't they happy? AI is reshaping developer roles, workflows and team culture.

AI use in software development is at an unusual stage of maturity. The overwhelming majority of developers are using AI tools to create code, but there are a lot of questions about the ramifications of doing so. How much should developers trust the code that AI produces? Where specifically does AI belong in the software development process? And what exactly is the role of software developers in the age of AI?

According to McKinsey’s The State of AI in 2026, 80% of AI users say that it has improved their individual productivity , and 50% say it helps them make better decisions. Yet there’s not a universally positive response from those who are making the most use of AI technology.

Some have pointed to a kind of AI “fatigue”, where developers managing multiple agents, juggling different tasks, and continually switching context are quickly overwhelmed.

Creating and maintaining a happy team is no small feat for any business. The way AI is changing the developer role makes it even trickier.

AI is often compared to a junior developer in its abilities. It follows, therefore, that those using AI are effectively managers, responsible for prompting the AI, checking in on progress, reviewing the output, and offering feedback where needed.

But most developers are not trained as managers, and even if they were, not all of the principles of management apply to AI agents. Some developers are finding the responsibility of managing multiple agents exhausting.

Part of this is from the sheer volume of code that AI is capable of producing. Running five agents at once will mean producing five times as much code. It seems very efficient, but it also means five times as much code that needs to be reviewed and approved.

Are you a pro? Subscribe to our newsletter

Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!

This isn’t really a new problem. We have more automation and convenience in our lives than ever before, from washing machines to automatic bill payment to delivery apps, but few people claim that they have too much free time.

The problem is not AI or convenience, but is wider, and systemic. In our daily lives, automation allowed us to take on other responsibilities, taking up the free time we were promised. In development teams, part of the problem is that the infrastructure and processes around AI have adapted, and bottlenecks have just shifted around.

AI tools have been built for one-to-one conversations and individual productivity. The pattern of adoption has reinforced this, as individuals experiment with AI tools in their own tasks, siloed away from everyone else. But that’s not how most modern development teams work.

The solution is not to automate review, but to make AI agents less like personal assistants and more like part of the team: running in the cloud , triggered by events as well as user prompts, running in the background where possible, and assisting across the whole workflow, such as in review and validation. The human team can then focus more on what they are better equipped to do, rather than micromanaging every AI task.

The shift in role shouldn’t be switching one type of drudgery for another, creating and refining prompts over and over instead of manually coding. The shift will be to one of scoping, architecture, and designing the system, not necessarily the code.

How do organizations measure success? Metrics such as “lines of code”…

items.title: For the first time, a C++ standard failed to pass the national bodies
items.content:
It looks like it happened! A historic first, for better or worse.

This is a sign that C++ is (still) struggling with its governance (see a

previous article on cultural issues within C++ here ). This is a big deal even if you do not care about programming languages. C++ is arguably the most

important programming language in existence.

Your computer runs on C or C++. The web browser you are using to read this is written in C++.

~All programming languages depend on C++ (often through LLVM). Likewise, ~all websites with performance

requirements (e.g. YouTube) depend on C++, ~all data storage, game engines, finance, etc.

In a world that is drowning in exciting new vulnerabilities in ~all software, the ability of C++ to change

and adjust to changing times affects you.

Let’s take a step back and get an overview. The initial source was a post by

"Balloting has completed for C++26. Unfortunately it was Disapproved. P-Members voting: 12 in

favor out of 20 = 60 % (requirement >= 66.66%) (P-Members having abstained are not counted in this

vote.) Member bodies voting: 9 negative votes out of 22 = 41 % (requirement

In a comment, J. Daniel García adds: “There were 12 countries that abstained. In several cases

because they could not reach to a common position. That is another signal of a contested draft.”

Now, before we get into the facts: This is not a good look for C++.

There have been multiple fights over the future direction of the C++ language, but no C++ standard ever

failed to be signed off by the national bodies.

The national body vote is considered to be a formality . By the time the vote reaches the national

bodies all disagreements should’ve been sorted out by WG21 (Working Group 21, i.e. the C++ Standards

Truly controversial features should never make it this far, since they should never be added to the C++26

working draft in the first place. This is a sign of division in the C++ community, in some form or

another, and completely independently of whether you agree with this result or not.

Here, “Added to the C++26 working draft” is essentially accepting the pull request. Everyone

is working towards the C++26 release, and people contribute to it with papers. Papers lead to votes, which

then lead to amendments of the draft. Finally (this is where we are) wording passes happen, and it gets

signed off, rubber-stamped and released. Phrased like this, the ISO process sounds sensible enough, but

trust me, it’s actually kind of a nightmare.

Needless to say, the debates are raging, with comments on all sides:

Wait, how did the voting break down? What are P-members???

Quick explanation: The national bodies execute a single vote. To pass the national bodies, the draft has

At least two-thirds of the participating voting members have to vote Yes .

At most one quarter of all voting members may vote No .

If the above posts are correct , then the draft failed to meet both bars. Twelve isn’t

two-thirds of twenty, and nine is more than a quarter. Visualization:

In total, there were 20 P-members, and 22 total members (ignoring abstaining). I heard that the US

abstained, but take that with a grain of salt.

tl;dr : WG21 voted to include Contracts in C++26. Several high-ranking members of

WG21 are strongly opposed to Contracts, and so are several national bodies. The national body vote was the

’last resort’ place to prevent Contracts from being canonicalized as part of the C++ standard.

Wait, that’s too fast for me, what are Contracts?

New keywords that replace assert macros with a standardized way to enforce runtime checks.

Most importantly, you can add pre and post checks to ensure that all arguments

and return values fulfill certain conditions.

This ends up looking roughly as follows:

pre (size > 0 ) // the caller must guarantee this

post ( r : 0 <= r && r < size) // the function promises this ; r is the return value

contract_assert(r >= 0 ); // a check inside the body

Looks simple, right? You’d think…

items.title: 글 쌌다 지웠다 하는 뷩쉰은 봐라
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

items.title: .name grandfathered
items.content:

This was a team effort. It was inspiring how many talented people joined this fight. From Doytchin who kicked everything off, to Jim who flew to Bali to make the case to ICANN in person, to Patrik, Troy, Huyen, Keith, Judy, Erik, and Ryan who wrote formal reconsideration requests, to my lawyers Jan, Flip and Diégo who threw the book at ICANN, to Beverly, Stefan, Vaughan, Irv, Pablo, Larry, Lionel, Daniel, Ori, Markus, Kirk, Ed, Jeremy, Stephan, Matija, Jan, Simon, Mark, and Evan who filed letters of support. I'd also like to sincerely thank selected individuals within ICANN who had the courage to stand up against the bureaucracy. Without exception, everyone I spoke with was a remarkable person.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Half of New Games on Steam Are Now Made With AI. How Does This Reflect the Gaming Industry?
items.content:
Steam's store doesn't look any different but if you dig into it, you'll start finding plenty of AI examples. Valve

Steam, the digital marketplace for PC games from game studio Valve, has hit a major milestone, sparking pushback from parts of the gaming community: Approximately 50% of new Steam games in October were made with the help of AI.

This underscores a growing trend in gaming , where more games are made with some form of AI assistance — specifically, generative AI, which developers have used to generate code, art assets, voice lines and more. Developers are adopting the technology in increasing numbers .

The numbers come from a Reddit user who goes by Ploz , and who used Steam’s publicly available data to see how many newly released games relied on AI in some capacity. This was possible because of Valve’s AI disclosure policy for newly released games, which requires developers to state whether they used AI in making their game. The disclosure is part of the storefront’s publicly accessible records, allowing anyone to view it.

A Valve representative did not respond to a request for comment.

The data is a snapshot of the tidal wave of AI-made games flooding storefronts, most prominently Steam. But crucially, Valve has chosen not to limit this flood, washing its hands of the problem and leaving gamers to fend for themselves in finding quality games. Developers had already been struggling to get their games noticed, and Valve’s limited curation seems completely unprepared for the firehose of AI-made games churned out on an increasing scale.

Valve implemented the AI disclosure policy in January 2024 to increase developer transparency. At the time, only 1.4% of newly released games used AI. This increased to 13.4% by the end of 2024, then to 24% by the end of 2025. It now sits at 49.9%.

There are some caveats. The AI disclosure is only required for games that use AI to create player-facing content, such as artwork, sound, character dialogue and localization. The 49.9% figure is specific to these types of games and doesn’t account for developers who use AI for behind-the-scenes tasks such as coding and bug fixes. A Google Cloud survey conducted in August 2025 showed that 87% of developers use AI for backend work, which doesn’t require disclosure on Steam.

So it’s likely that the number of games on Steam built with AI assistance is greater than 50%. Ploz notes that the only way users can avoid AI-generated games is to manually check for AI disclosures.

Many developers had more than one of those areas named in their disclosure, and about a quarter of developers said they were using AI for their Steam store pages and marketing.

About 3% of developers used AI directly as a game mechanic. One such example is a driving simulator called Teach My Little Sister How to Drive . Developers use AI in the game to interpret a player’s voice commands and generate the sister’s responses. items.title: Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming?
items.content:
Last week, MIT CSAIL published Sparks of Weight-Space Programming . Given the raw weights of a small network, GPT-6 Astra could tell which game it had been trained to play. Given only a game’s rules, it could write the weights of a small network from scratch and beat networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. No gradients, no training loop, just reasoning about what the weights compute. They coined this weight-space programming .

In another experiment, they asked Astra to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math by editing its weights. Astra changed only 0.016% of the weights, and MATH-500 accuracy jumped from 7.9% to 48.1%. 1

Looking at Astra’s edit, I realized most of its search was solving a linear program by trial and error. It spent about 8 hours and 28 forward passes choosing which weights to change and by how much. A couple of LP solves, about a minute each, do the same job with 8× fewer changed weights. In this post I’ll walk through the edit, why it’s an LP, and what that says about the fix itself.

Small reasoning models have a common failure: they get stuck in thinking loops , repeating the same few lines over and over instead of finishing their reasoning. Qwen3.5-0.8B is especially prone to it, and its model card says so. On MATH-500, 93% of the base model’s answers ran into the 32,768-token limit without ever reaching an answer.

The edit fixes the loops, so it helps anywhere the model loops. That includes instruction following: IFEval went from 21% to 62%.

Qwen3.5-0.8B MATH-500 GSM8K IFEval Hit token limit

On Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops, Astra couldn’t meaningfully improve its math ability. As the authors put it, editing the weights could remove an obstacle hiding an ability, but couldn’t add one the model lacked.

Transformers use residual connections: each layer’s output is added to its input rather than replacing it. Follow one token through the network and you get a single vector that every layer adds to, called the residual stream (1,024-dimensional in this model). When the model is looping, the residual stream shifts in a consistent direction. Astra’s fix was to edit two layers so that what they add points the opposite way.

Astra wrote four pairs of short texts, each a piece of productive reasoning and a looping version of the same reasoning. It ran all eight through the model and recorded each token’s residual stream vector at one layer. Averaging over the looping texts gives one vector, and averaging over the productive texts gives another. Their difference, normalized, is the loop direction $u$: the way the residual stream moves when the model loops.

Each MLP ends with a matrix $W$ (called down_proj ). At every token, it turns the MLP’s 3,584-dimensional hidden activation $h$ into a 1,024-dimensional output $Wh$, which gets added to the residual stream $x$:

$$x \leftarrow x + Wh, \qquad Wh = \sum_j h_j \, w_j$$ So the MLP’s output is always a weighted sum of the same 3,584 vectors, the columns $w_j$ of $W$. $W$ fixes what those vectors are; the activations $h_j$ decide how much of each one gets added at each token.

Each column points partly along $u$. That amount, $u^\top w_j$, is how much column $j$ pushes the model toward looping whenever $h_j$ is active. Astra’s edit subtracts a multiple $\alpha$ of it:

$$w_j \to w_j - \alpha \, (u^\top w_j) \, u$$ At $\alpha = 1$ the component along $u$ is gone, so the column no longer pushes toward looping. Doing this to every column in layers 15 and 19 took accuracy from 9% to 33% on GSM8K and MATH training problems. At $\alpha = 6$ the component is flipped: a column that wrote $+a$ along $u$ now writes $-5a$, and pushes the model away from looping whenever it’s used.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
items.content:
United Airlines said on Wednesday that it is banning artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing  security risks  and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules.

Many consumers are turning to AI agents such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots to complete tasks ranging from researching products and tracking down deals to making purchases.

To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."

The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances.

"As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.

United's new policy suggests the company wants to retain control over the customer booking process, said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group.

"United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."

Other airlines are taking a different tack to the emergence of AI agents. For example, Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can access the airline's website through the AI app.

United fares will continue to be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, adding that "consumers shouldn't find it any more difficult to find good fares on the airline."

"But by blocking the AI bots, United won't make it any easier to find its fares, either," he said.

where an attacker points a previously safe tag at malicious code.

For example, an old workflow looks like:

on : [ push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch]

- uses : j178/prek-action@44924fe9ef4a6f88253c4b6b1bf11c689d3ce53d # v3.1.0

$ gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock

items.summary_ko: GitHub Actions는 태그가 바뀔 수 있어 전체 커밋 SHA로 고정하라는 권장이 있었다. 이 글은 gh-actions-lock 확장을 사용해 워크플로에는 vX.Y.Z 태그를 쓰고, 커밋 SHA는 actions.lock 파일에 기록하는 방법을 소개한다. 수정된 워크플로와 새 lockfile을 함께 커밋하라고 안내한다.
items.content_ko: 기존에는 GitHub Actions를 태그 대신 전체 커밋 SHA로 고정하라고 권장해 왔다. 태그는 바뀔 수 있어서, 공격자가 예전에 안전했던 태그를 악성 코드가 담긴 커밋으로 가리키게 만들 수 있기 때문이다. 이 글은 gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock으로 확장을 설치한 뒤, 워크플로 파일은 vX.Y.Z 태그를 쓰는 방식으로 바꾸는 과정을 보여준다. 그러면 gh actions-lock 명령이 .github/workflows/actions.lock 파일을 생성하고, 여기에 커밋 SHA가 기록된다. 이 파일은 기계가 생성하는 것이므로 직접 편집하지 말고 명령으로 갱신하라고 안내한다. 마지막으로 수정된 워크플로와 새 lockfile을 함께 커밋하라고 권한다. 원문이 중간에서 잘려 있다.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: UK Under-16 Social Media Ban Could Hit YouTube Kids, Spotify
items.content:

The UK under-16 social media ban is about to get much bigger. In fact, new reports say ministers want the rules to cover recommender systems and user-generated content. As a result, YouTube Kids, Lego Play and even Spotify could fall under the ban. Up to 150 platforms could face the new restrictions.

The government announced its plan to stop children under 16 from using social media in June 2026. At first, most people expected the ban to target big names like Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat. Now, however, the working proposal looks far wider. Ministers expect to finalise the regulations this week, but the final text remains private.

Key Points The government wants a “catch-all” rule built around recommender systems and user-generated content.

Up to 150 platforms could fall in scope, including YouTube Kids, Lego Play and possibly Spotify.

Platforms may get an “off ramp”: they can remove harmful features and leave the ban’s scope.

However, tech industry groups say YouTube Kids cannot work without its recommendation engine.

The ban should start around March, and the regulations should reach Parliament by the end of 2026.

What Is Changing in the UK Under-16 Social Media Ban?

The first plan focused on social networks, where people post, share and chat. Now the working proposal looks at what a service does, not just what it calls itself. It targets two things. First, it targets recommender systems, the algorithms that suggest videos, songs or posts. Second, it targets user-generated content, which means anything users upload or share.

This wider net matters because many apps now use some form of recommendation or user content. As one industry voice put it, the whole internet has a recommender system. For this reason, services that never called themselves social media now sit in the danger zone.

The main reason is workarounds. Australia started its own under-16 ban in December 2025. Since then, critics say teenagers quickly moved to new apps or found other ways to message friends on harmless-looking sites. Therefore, UK ministers want to avoid a repeat. A broad definition leaves fewer gaps, so children find it harder to simply switch platforms.

The government delivers the ban through secondary legislation under the Online Safety Act 2023. It uses powers that the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 added. Ofcom, the UK online safety regulator, will enforce the rules. For the full details, read the official GOV.UK consultation response .

YouTube Kids, Lego Play and Spotify: Who Could Fall in Scope?

YouTube Kids Many people saw it as safe because it targets children. However, it runs on a recommendation engine, so it could now fall in scope.

Lego Play This games platform offers interactive features and suggestions. Therefore, the rules could treat it as a games and social space.

Spotify It shows recommended songs and podcasts and hosts some user content. Still, it wants reassurance that it does not count as a social platform.

eBay and Vinted These marketplaces let users message each other. Also, the culture secretary says the government is looking seriously at retail sites.

Industry groups warn that YouTube Kids stops working properly without its recommender system. Consequently, the off ramp looks almost impossible to use. Lego Play faces a similar problem, because its experience depends on suggestions and interaction.

Marketplaces add another twist. For example, eBay already asks all members to be 18 or older. Vinted, on the other hand, has around 17 million UK users and lets parents open supervised accounts for children.

The “Off Ramp”: How Platforms Could Escape the Ban
